label: S-A2 wrong key: same extension, double k stores double the energy; key says the same

item.question_text: Springs X and Y are stretched by the same extension. Spring X has twice the spring constant of spring Y. How does the energy stored in X compare with Y? Use \(E_e = \tfrac{1}{2}ke^{2}\).

options.c: X stores four times as much

feedback.a: The extension is the same, so the energy stored is the same.
feedback.c: Only the extension is squared, and it is the same for both.
feedback.d: A spring with a smaller spring constant does not store more energy for the same extension.

misconception_map.a: slip: thinks the spring constant changes the energy
misconception_map.d: slip: inverted the relationship with k

item.explanation: With the same extension, both springs store the same energy.

label: S-B2 outside the boundary: Ee = ½ke² applied beyond the limit of proportionality

item.question_text: A spring with a spring constant of \(100\,\text{N/m}\) is stretched beyond its limit of proportionality, to an extension of \(0.3\,\text{m}\). Calculate the energy stored in its elastic potential energy store. Use \(E_e = \tfrac{1}{2}ke^{2}\).

wrong.misconception: This does not square the extension: \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 100 \times 0.3^{2} = 4.5\,\text{J}\).

label: S-B1/C1 mastery check that tests unit recall (not elastic energy), with a filler option (kg)

item.question_text: In which unit is the spring constant of a spring measured?

feedback.b: Joules measure energy, not the spring constant.
feedback.c: Newtons measure force; the spring constant is force per metre of extension.

misconception_map.c: slip: gave the unit of force
misconception_map.d: slip: gave the unit of mass

item.explanation: The spring constant is the force needed per metre of extension, so its unit is N/m.
